title: How Long Does a Knee Replacement Last? What the Long-Term Data Shows
metaDescription: Most knee replacements are still working 15 to 25 years on. What the registry data really measures, why implants fail, and what you can do to protect yours.
intro: "How many years will it last?" is one of the first things people ask before agreeing to a knee replacement. The honest answer is that most last a very long time, but no one can promise a number for your knee. The figures below come from large joint registries, and it helps to know what they do and do not measure.

sections.heading: How long does a knee replacement last?
sections.body: Most total knee replacements last well beyond 15 years. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons says more than 90% of modern knee replacements are still functioning well at 15 years. A large pooled analysis of long-term data found that about 82% were still in place at 25 years. These are group averages, not a guarantee for any one person.

sections.heading: What do the 25-year figures actually mean?
sections.body: The 82% figure comes from a 2019 meta-analysis of case series and national registries, and the 25-year result rests mainly on the Finnish registry (76,651 knees). "Lasting" there means no second operation was needed. A knee that is stiff or sore but was never revised still counts as a success, so the figure says little about comfort or satisfaction. The case series were also judged to be of low quality, and the authors did not analyse by implant generation, so today's implants may behave differently. Implants followed for 25 years were necessarily implanted 25 years ago, so these figures describe past designs rather than what is used today.

sections.heading: Why do knee replacements fail?
sections.body: The usual reasons are wear of the plastic spacer, loosening of the implant from the bone, infection, instability, stiffness caused by scar tissue, and fractures around the implant after a fall. Wear is expected over time and is not a defect. Infection is uncommon, reported by the AAOS in fewer than 2% of patients, but it can appear weeks or years after surgery and sometimes means the implant has to come out.
bullets: Wear and loosening: gradual, and often the reason for revision in later years
Infection: can occur at any time, including years later
Instability and stiffness: can be treated with bracing, physiotherapy or manipulation first, and revision only if those fail
Fracture around the implant: typically from a fall

sections.heading: Do my weight and activity change how long it lasts?
sections.body: Yes, within limits. The AAOS notes that excessive activity or body weight can speed wear and may cause the implant to loosen and become painful. Surgeons generally advise avoiding running and jumping for life, while walking, swimming, cycling, golf and light hiking are fine. In practice this is the part you control: keeping your weight in a healthy range, staying active in low-impact ways, and preventing falls, especially in the first few weeks after surgery.

sections.heading: What happens if my knee replacement wears out or loosens?
sections.body: A revision operation replaces some or all of the implant. It is a longer and more complex procedure than the first one, with a higher risk of complications and a slower recovery, and infection risk is slightly higher. Most people who need one still do well, with better pain relief, stability and function, but complete pain relief is not always achieved. A knee that becomes newly painful, swollen or unstable years after surgery should be assessed rather than put up with.

sections.heading: Does a partial knee replacement last as long as a total one?
sections.body: The pooled data suggest not quite: about 70% of partial replacements were still in place at 25 years, against 82% for total replacements. That does not make partial replacement the wrong choice. It suits a limited pattern of arthritis in one part of the knee, and the trade-off is a somewhat higher chance of needing further surgery later. The 25-year partial figure rests on fewer patients, so treat it as approximate. Which operation fits depends on an examination and X-rays, not on these averages.

sections.heading: How will I know if something is wrong years later?
sections.body: New pain, swelling, warmth, a feeling of the knee giving way, or a knee that gradually stiffens are all reasons to be reviewed, even if surgery was years ago. Fever with a hot, red, swollen knee needs same-day care because infection can threaten the implant. Ask your own surgeon what follow-up they recommend. Early review makes treatment simpler.

sections.heading: Should I delay surgery so the implant lasts longer?
sections.body: Not for that reason alone. Waiting to protect the implant means living longer with pain and reduced walking, and the registry data cannot tell you how much a delay would help your own knee. The better question is whether arthritis is limiting your life now, and whether non-surgical treatment has had a fair trial. If it has, the timing is a conversation about your symptoms, fitness and goals, not about a countdown on the implant.

faqs.q: How many years does a knee replacement last?
faqs.a: Most last well beyond 15 years: the AAOS reports more than 90% of modern knee replacements still working well at 15 years, and a pooled analysis found about 82% still in place at 25 years. These are averages for groups of patients and not a promise for any one knee.

faqs.q: Can a knee replacement last 25 years or more?
faqs.a: Yes, for many people. A 2019 pooled analysis led by the University of Bristol found about 82% of total knee replacements were still in place at 25 years. The evidence is mostly from older implants and from registry data, so it describes past results rather than a guarantee.

faqs.q: What shortens the life of a knee replacement?
faqs.a: Wear of the plastic spacer, loosening, infection, instability and fractures after falls. The AAOS says excessive activity or body weight can speed wear and loosening, and advises avoiding running and jumping.

faqs.q: What happens when a knee replacement needs revision?
faqs.a: The worn or loosened parts are replaced in a second operation. Revision is longer and more complex than the first surgery, with higher complication risk and slower recovery, though most patients still get good pain relief and function.

faqs.q: Should I put off knee replacement so it lasts longer?
faqs.a: Not on that basis alone. Delaying means longer living with pain, and the registry data cannot show how much a delay would extend the life of your implant. The decision should rest on your symptoms and how far non-surgical care has helped.

footerNote: If knee pain is limiting your walking, stairs or sleep, read about knee replacement, the question of delaying surgery, the non-surgical options and recovery after knee replacement, or book a consultation. A hot, red, very swollen knee with fever, or a new replacement that suddenly becomes painful or unstable, needs same-day medical care.
